clue.text: Occupied with abridged Sinclair

indicators.note: abridged means shortened, so the surname loses its final letter

parts.note: Upton Sinclair was the American novelist who wrote The Jungle

explanation.surface: Someone busy reading a shortened edition of an Upton Sinclair novel.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface makes Sinclair a surname, but the wordplay needs his first name, Upton; 'abridged' drops its last letter.
explanation.definitionFit: To be up to something is to be busy or engaged in it, an idiom for being occupied.

clue.text: Small amount from Butler

definitions.meaning: as much as a penny buys, a small quantity
Alfred, the butler to Batman, has this surname

explanation.definitionFit: A pennyworth is a tiny quantity, and the same word is the surname of Bruce Wayne's manservant Alfred.

clue.text: Map-makers supported angry young man

parts.note: OS is the Ordnance Survey, Britain's official map-making body
borne means carried or held up

explanation.surface: Cartographers backing a furious youth.
explanation.walkthrough: The Angry Young Men were a group of 1950s British writers; John Osborne wrote Look Back in Anger.
explanation.definitionFit: The playwright John Osborne was the leading figure among the 1950s writers labelled the Angry Young Men.

clue.text: Must Collins somehow save liberal members of the press?

indicators.note: somehow says these letters come together in some other order
save here means except, so one letter is left out of the words

explanation.surface: A demand that Collins rescue the progressive journalists.
explanation.walkthrough: 'save' means 'except': drop one L from MUSTCOLLINS, then 'somehow' rearranges the remaining ten letters.
explanation.definitionFit: Writers who contribute regular opinion pieces to newspapers are journalists, members of the press.

clue.text: Revolutionary Bodyguard musical

parts.note: Che Guevara is the archetypal revolutionary in crosswords
the SS was originally Hitler's bodyguard unit

explanation.surface: A stage show about a rebel's protection officer.
explanation.walkthrough: Chess is the 1980s musical by Tim Rice with the men of ABBA.
explanation.definitionFit: Chess is the title of a stage musical about a Cold War chess match.

clue.text: Nobel laureate, British, out of favour

indicators.note: out of says one letter is removed from the longer word

parts.note: a blessing is a favour or boon

explanation.surface: A Nobel prize-winner, British-born, who has fallen from grace.
explanation.walkthrough: 'out of favour' looks like one phrase meaning disgraced, but 'out of' tells you to take B from BLESSING.
explanation.definitionFit: Doris Lessing won the Nobel Prize in Literature in 2007.

clue.text: Bloom's pen name hurt? I agree with it

parts.note: to mar is to damage or spoil
yes expresses agreement
it is an old slang term for sex appeal

explanation.surface: Someone asking whether Bloom's pseudonym was a painful one, then nodding along.
explanation.walkthrough: Not Leopold or Molly Bloom: the romantic novelist Ursula Bloom also published as Mary Essex.
explanation.definitionFit: The prolific novelist Ursula Bloom wrote some books under this pseudonym.

clue.text: Male desperately chasing sea creature, following lead character?

indicators.note: chasing puts the scrambled word after the other piece
only the letters that follow the lead letter are kept, so the first one goes

parts.note: a fish is a sea creature

indicators.note: desperately suggests wild disorder, so these letters are jumbled

explanation.surface: A man frantically pursuing a sea animal, behind someone in charge.
explanation.walkthrough: The sea creature evokes Moby-Dick, whose narrator opens 'Call me Ishmael'. 'desperately' turns MALE into MAEL.
explanation.definitionFit: Ishmael is the narrating figure of Melville's whaling novel, a fictional person in a book.

clue.text: Quickly move nickname for David Copperfield

definitions.meaning: to go at a brisk running pace
his aunt Betsey Trotwood calls him by a shortened form of her surname

explanation.definitionFit: To trot is to go at a jog, and Dickens's Aunt Betsey calls her nephew by this pet name.

clue.text: In Spain, The Trial overturned sanction

indicators.note: overturned says the whole run of letters is turned back to front

parts.note: el is the Spanish word for the
a bane is a trial or affliction

explanation.surface: Kafka's novel The Trial banned and then reprieved in Spain.
explanation.walkthrough: The Trial suggests Kafka, but 'Trial' means a nuisance; 'overturned' reverses ELBANE.
explanation.definitionFit: To sanction something is to authorise or permit it, to make it possible.

clue.text: Outlaw behind rejection of most of modern slavery

indicators.note: behind puts the outlaw after the other piece
rejection suggests sending back, so the shortened word is reversed
most of says the word is cut short by its final letter

parts.note: fresh means new or modern
Robin Hood is the archetypal English outlaw

explanation.surface: A bandit rebelling against present-day forced labour.
explanation.walkthrough: 'modern' as FRESH is a looser synonym than it looks; 'rejection of' turns the shortened word round, and 'behind' sets Robin Hood after it.
explanation.definitionFit: Serfdom, the condition of a feudal labourer bound to the land, is a kind of bondage.

clue.text: In Wuthering Heights, Joseph's raving: no one remarks, outside of Hindley

indicators.note: raving means wild, so the letters are jumbled

parts.note: taken as written
I is the Roman numeral for one

indicators.note: outside of picks the first and last letters of the name

explanation.surface: Joseph in Wuthering Heights ranting so that no one comments, beyond Hindley.
explanation.walkthrough: Joseph is the dour Yorkshire servant at Wuthering Heights. 'raving' shuffles NO, I, REMARKS and HY, the first and last letters of Hindley.
explanation.definitionFit: Joseph, the grumbling servant in Emily Bronte's novel, speaks broad dialect as a man from the Yorkshire moors.

clue.text: "And who so happy, — O who, / As the Duck and the Kangaroo?" (The Duck and the Kangaroo, -)

definitions.text: "And who so happy, — O who, / As the Duck and the Kangaroo?" (The Duck and the Kangaroo, -)

parts.words: "And who so happy, — O who, / As the Duck and the Kangaroo?" (The Duck and the Kangaroo, -)
parts.note: a quotation with its source given, and the poet's name left blank for the solver to supply

explanation.definitionFit: The nonsense poem The Duck and the Kangaroo was written by the Victorian poet famous for limericks.

clue.text: Where to put notes in bogeyman novel

indicators.note: novel means new, so the letters take a new arrangement

explanation.surface: A place to store a book about a scary monster.
explanation.walkthrough: 'novel' looks like a noun, a book about a bogeyman, but it signals the anagram.
explanation.definitionFit: Banknotes are kept in a money bag, a pouch for cash.

clue.text: Book breaks between flights for Wodehousian site

parts.note: landings are the level stretches between flights of stairs

explanation.surface: A novel interrupting the time between plane journeys at a Wodehouse location.
explanation.walkthrough: Blandings Castle is the setting of many P. G. Wodehouse novels; 'flights' are of stairs, not aeroplanes.
explanation.definitionFit: Blandings Castle, home of Lord Emsworth, is a recurring setting in P. G. Wodehouse's fiction.

clue.text: Some with a captain for long-running Journey's End

indicators.note: Some says the answer is a run of letters hidden inside the words that follow

parts.note: the letters run across the end of one word into the next

explanation.surface: Part of a ship's crew on a voyage that has dragged on, nearing the end.
explanation.walkthrough: The 'long-running journey' is the Odyssey, which lasts ten years and ends with Odysseus home in Ithaca; the captain is Odysseus.
explanation.definitionFit: Ithaca, Odysseus's island home, is where Homer's epic voyage finally ends.

clue.text: A court decision blocking The Running Man

indicators.note: blocking puts one piece inside another, obstructing it

parts.note: taken as written
a let is a ruling in tennis that a point be replayed

explanation.surface: A judge's ruling stopping the film The Running Man.
explanation.walkthrough: The 'court' is a tennis court, not a law court: a LET is called when a serve clips the net.
explanation.definitionFit: A runner in races, such as a sprinter, is a sportsman, a man who runs.

clue.text: Like dystopian author of colour, around 40, Scotsman?

indicators.note: around says the colour word goes round the number

parts.note: a hue is a shade of colour
XL is 40 in Roman numerals
Ian is a typical Scottish man's name

explanation.surface: A question about whether a dystopian novelist was a stout Scot of about forty.
explanation.walkthrough: Aldous Huxley wrote the dystopia Brave New World.
explanation.definitionFit: Huxleian describes something in the manner of Aldous Huxley, author of Brave New World.

clue.text: Lively character's husband, a politican not for turning

parts.note: H is the abbreviation for husband in family trees
MP, Member of Parliament, is a politician

indicators.note: for turning says the word is read backwards

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: Echoes Thatcher's 'The lady's not for turning', about a politician's husband.
explanation.walkthrough: 'not for turning' is Margaret Thatcher's famous phrase; here it reverses NOT. 'Lively' is the novelist Penelope Lively.
explanation.definitionFit: A figure in a novel by Penelope Lively bears this surname.

clue.text: Scholarly article ultimately unpleasant about computing

indicators.note: ultimately points to the final letter of the word
about says one piece wraps round the other

parts.note: rude means coarse or unpleasant
IT is information technology, that is computing

explanation.surface: A learned paper ends up being nasty about computer science.
explanation.walkthrough: 'ultimately' takes E, the last letter of 'article'.
explanation.definitionFit: Erudite means deeply learned, as a scholar is.

clue.text: Thud made dent to War and Peace book

indicators.note: to here works as a shift, telling the letters to change into a new order

explanation.surface: A heavy blow dented a copy of Tolstoy's novel.
explanation.walkthrough: The 'Peace' book is by David Peace, whose novel about Brian Clough's war at Leeds United is The Damned Utd.
explanation.definitionFit: David Peace's novel about Brian Clough's turbulent 44 days at Leeds United bears this title.

clue.text: Lines omitting any English, after European drama

indicators.note: after puts the shortened word behind the other piece
omitting any English means every E is left out

parts.note: queues are lines of people waiting

explanation.surface: A play stripped of its English after going through Europe.
explanation.walkthrough: 'omitting any English' removes both Es from QUEUES, leaving QUUS. Equus is a play by Peter Shaffer.
explanation.definitionFit: Equus is Peter Shaffer's 1973 stage play about a boy who blinds horses.

clue.text: Millions supporting remote setting for Orwell or Gibbons

indicators.note: in a down clue a supporting piece sits underneath, so the millions letter goes last

parts.note: far means distant or remote

explanation.surface: Millions backing a remote location for two novelists.
explanation.walkthrough: Orwell wrote Animal Farm; Stella Gibbons wrote Cold Comfort Farm.
explanation.definitionFit: Animal Farm and Cold Comfort Farm both take place on an agricultural holding.

clue.text: Small snack of rabbit head

parts.note: Hazel is the rabbit who leads the warren in Watership Down
nut is slang for the head

explanation.surface: A tiny treat made from a rabbit's head.
explanation.walkthrough: 'rabbit head' suggests a gory dish; Hazel is the lead rabbit in Richard Adams's Watership Down.
explanation.definitionFit: A hazelnut is a small nut eaten as a snack.

clue.text: Blake's original figure is lurid, naked, and meditative

indicators.note: naked means stripped, so the word loses its first and last letters

parts.note: Zen is the meditative school of Buddhism

explanation.surface: Describes a Blake creation as garish, nude and lost in thought.
explanation.walkthrough: 'naked' strips LURID of its first and last letters, leaving URI. Urizen is the primeval lawgiver in Blake's mythology.
explanation.definitionFit: Urizen is the primordial creator-god of William Blake's prophetic books.

clue.text: Oddball pens dramas for characters from Romeo & Juliet and Troilus & Cressida

definitions.text: characters from Romeo & Juliet and Troilus & Cressida

indicators.note: oddball suggests something eccentric, so the letters are rearranged

explanation.surface: An eccentric writes plays, two of Shakespeare's among them.
explanation.walkthrough: 'characters' are printed symbols, not people: the & in each title.
explanation.definitionFit: The & sign in each title is a typographic symbol standing for 'and'.

clue.text: Cockney regularly shelters governess

indicators.note: shelters says the answer is held inside the words that follow

explanation.surface: A Londoner often gives shelter to a children's tutor.
explanation.walkthrough: 'regularly' looks like an alternate-letters signal but is just part of the hiding place.
explanation.definitionFit: Jane Eyre, Charlotte Bronte's heroine, works as a governess at Thornfield.
